I spoke with David Harley from Intelligentvision the other night on the phone for about an hour.  Really nice guy.  He gave me plenty of advice on how to distribute homebrew games.

I gave David the measurements of the Astrocade cartridge.  He thinks that it will fit perfectly inside their Intellivision homebrew box.  He will be sending me a sample box so that I can check this out.  If it does fit well, then there is a way for us to get printed boxes for a fee that will be reasonable, though it will have to be done with my order "tagging" along with one of their orders.  I'll keep you informed on how this works out.

David does have some other advice for me as well:

1) Collect emails for potential buyers.  This contradicts what I just said a couple of days ago when someone asked to be put on a pre-order list (and I said their isn't one).  However, his reasoning seems quite sound and I'm going to try to figure-out the best way to do this.  This will probably require server-side scripting.  Lance, is this available to Bally Alley?  If it is available, can you help me use it?

2) I've worked with Pay Pal (of course) for purchasing and selling items on Ebay, but I wasn't sure how easy it would be to use when selling these cartridges.  He says its as easy a putting a button on the webpage.  The Pay Pal charge is about 3.5% of the price the item is sold for (if the item sells for about $50-- it may change at other prices).

3) He has used digital printing for boxes in the past.  He says that in comparison that 4-color printing is FAR superior.

4) I mentioned offhandedly that I wouldn't have much trouble creating the box or manual (minus the illustration) because I have already created covers for the George Moses audio CDs that I made for myself.  He suggests that I try selling them.  He says that this will bring interest plus get me people's email addresses who might be interested in the cartridge.  I always wanted to sell the CDs, but I want them professionally made (i.e. not burned).  Does anyone know the best way to do this?  I've checked into this before (locally) but could never find a reasonable price (given how small the distribution would be).

5) He suggests that I start a blog about the cartridge.  I'm not sure of the best way to do this either.  I've brought this up in the past, but I never have made the blog.  Perhaps this will give me the motivation to really check out the best way to do it.

Comments?

Ok, one more time 
The old tube type TV's were very sensitive to outside interference. With the
"Rabbit Ear" antennas that were extremely popular then, the chance of
interfering with a TV within your house was really great. Ask me how I know!
With today's digital  tuners (made with IC's rather than tubes, they have a
better rejection to outside interference. If February of '09 (not really
that far away),  all sets will HAVE to have a digital tuner of some sort.
ALL new sets have them built in. The older sets will need an external tuner.
These tuners will NOT be able to receive the analog signal that our Bally /
Astrocade units transmit. In conclusion, the small amount of "transmission"
from an uncovered unit will be of no consequence to anyone then.
HOWEVER, if you live in an apartment building in a metropolitan area, you or
your neighbors TV may still have rabbit ears on it and you could interfere
with channels 2-5 with your unit until February.
Ken

5766:
Here it is, the totally unofficial but totally brief:



COLOR BASIC manual
<http://tech.groups.yahoo.com/group/ballyalley/files/COLOR%20BASIC%20man\
ual.txt>


Color BASIC is based on the original Bally BASIC, including the 300 baud
interface code, with a couple of exceptions.  There are now only EIGHT
lines (by 26 characters) of text available on screen.  However you can
set the Background Color and the Foreground Color for each of these
lines separately now!  The bottom 5/13ths of the screen (as well as the
border) is the same color as the top line - and hides the Basic listing.
Although a smaller size is actually usable, the code runs much faster
since there is no need to interlace it with (and un-interlace it from)
the screen display!!

There are only two new commands to learn (and no, CLINE doesn't draw
colored lines, sorry):

COLOR - sets the colors of one of eight 4-color palettes for use by the
EIGHT interrupt routines that occur each sixtieth of a second.  Defaults
are all White except for the first one, which has Black for the
foreground text characters.
Usage is WORD-shift then BACKSPACE using a regular Basic overlay to get
COLOR a,b,c,d,e - where 'a' is the palette number from 1 to 7, and the
others are the regular colors from 0 to 255 for the background,
foreground, plus two more un-named colors which can be now be displayed
by the regular BOX and LINE routines.

CLINE - chooses the palette to be used by each line of text.  There is a
little bit of jitter when the colors change in MESS, which may or may
not be present on a real Bally/Astrocade machine.  All lines may have
their own palette or they can also share, and default to the first
black-on-white color set.
WORD-shift then SPACE for CLINE n,a - where 'n' is the line number 1
through 7 from the top, and 'a' corresponds to an 'a' as used in the
Color command.

Programs can now simply ramp the colors in the palettes or shuffle the
line colors around for fascinating rainbow effects.  {Submissions
accepted}.

>
> Color BASIC is based on the original Bally BASIC, including the 300 baud
> interface code, with a couple of exceptions.  There are now only EIGHT
> lines (by 26 characters) of text available on screen.  However you can
> set the Background Color and the Foreground Color for each of these
> lines separately now!  The bottom 5/13ths of the screen (as well as the
> border) is the same color as the top line - and hides the Basic listing.
> Although a smaller size is actually usable, the code runs much faster
> since there is no need to interlace it with (and un-interlace it from)
> the screen display!!
>
> There are only two new commands to learn (and no, CLINE doesn't draw
> colored lines, sorry):
>
> COLOR - sets the colors of one of eight 4-color palettes for use by the
> EIGHT interrupt routines that occur each sixtieth of a second.  Defaults
> are all White except for the first one, which has Black for the
> foreground text characters.
> Usage is WORD-shift then BACKSPACE using a regular Basic overlay to get
> COLOR a,b,c,d,e - where 'a' is the palette number from 1 to 7, and the
> others are the regular colors from 0 to 255 for the background,
> foreground, plus two more un-named colors which can be now be displayed
> by the regular BOX and LINE routines.
>
> CLINE - chooses the palette to be used by each line of text.  There is a
> little bit of jitter when the colors change in MESS, which may or may
> not be present on a real Bally/Astrocade machine.  All lines may have
> their own palette or they can also share, and default to the first
> black-on-white color set.
> WORD-shift then SPACE for CLINE n,a - where 'n' is the line number 1
> through 7 from the top, and 'a' corresponds to an 'a' as used in the
> Color command.
>
> Programs can now simply ramp the colors in the palettes or shuffle the
> line colors around for fascinating rainbow effects.  {Submissions
> accepted}.
>

This was a reply to Ken Lill because I thought he wanted to program a
game from scratch, but he wanted to go in a different direction.  As
long as I typed it up I thought someone could take it and run with it:

That sounds like the perfect game for YOU to write to show off the "new"
Color BASIC's special features! There's four different colors you can
use in each of eight different stripes - plus another four on the right
side that are unaffected by the interrupts (currently they are set to
black).

You could have the top one(s) sky/cloud colored - only moving the clouds
occasionally would be enough for people to say "Wow, movement!"  Below,
sky/grass plus a color for your character. Then the rest could be brown
and gold plus the character color.  Use the last stripe for the scores,
since below that would be sky blue anyway.  Flashing any level's colors
would be simple, and maybe you could have the grass layer drop down as
the dirt is mined out below it.  Let me know if you'll need any variable
addresses.  PRINT SZ only showed about 1024 bytes free, is that enough?

Wasn't sure if BOX and LINE really drew in the four colors, but you can
try them.  Overall speed might not actually be faster - those interrupts
will take some time away.  After it's all been written in Basic, then
converting to assembly code _might_ be possible (as ARTillery DUEL was).

The fastest way to get it into a cartridge, though, would be to burn the
listing after a copy of COLOR Basic, the way that the BALLY BASIC DEMO
videocade was done.  You'd need an 8K EPROM, and somebody to burn it...

of the original BALLY Basic (and COLOR Basic since it is so similar).
Naturally the old 300 baud comments are not included in that. Of course,
if somebody did have the assembly listing of the first Basic with
comments then I just wasted the last couple of weeks doing that...

in COLOR Basic, but that just might have to be one of those things.  All
that flashing of the screen background was pretty annoying anyway, as I
remember.

If you know the z-80 Machine Code, it shouldn't be too hard to switch to assembly. Just substituting the text name for the ## codes.

Except for ORG you can pretty much ignore the DEFs and such. They are just to assign numbers to words making it easier to read the code and remember for the average programmer. You can always use the numbers directly.

You can look at the programming samples .asm files to get an idea. And/or run them through ZMAC and look at the .lst file showing both the ML and neumonics.

5788:
Lance F. Squire wrote:
> > Except for ORG you can pretty much ignore the DEFs and such. They are > just to assign numbers to words making it easier to read the code and > remember for the average programmer.

DOH!!!!

Just as I was putting my little girl to sleep I realised I was confusing EQUates with DEFines.

DEFineBytes (DEFB) is your best friend when using strings of text. Here is an example:

LABEL	DEFB	'BALL TEST',0	;NULL DELIMITED STRINGS
LABEL2	DEFB	'3 BALL TEST',0
LABEL3	DEFB	'BLANK',0

These are labels for menu items on my ProgramTest3.z80 (.asm) file. The assembler turns that into:

  31:	2013  42414C4C	LABEL	DEFB	'BALL TEST',0	;NULL DELIMITED STRINGS
	      20544553
	      5400
  32:	201D  33204241	LABEL2	DEFB	'3 BALL TEST',0
	      4C4C2054
	      45535400
  33:	2029  424C414E	LABEL3	DEFB	'BLANK',0
	      4B00

As you can see the 42414C4C in line 31 is the ASCII for BALL.

I beleave this would much faster than using a Monitor program to enter the text.

I hope this helps.

5802:
I found thirteen videos that use the Datamax UV-1 on Youtube.  The UV-1 computer (basically, a beefed-up, very expensive Astrocade) was used in the early eighties.  Some of these videos try pretty hard to be "artsy," so bare with them.  Also, most of the videos seem incomplete; only the first minute or minute and a half are shown.

All of these video were uploaded by Electronic Visualization Laboratory (EVL)

http://www.youtube.com/user/evltube

Check 'em out.  I look forward to your comments.

Adam


Drive or Be Driven
(1984)
     This is an early example of electronic art design created at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory at the University of Illinois at Chicago by Dana Plepys (MFA alumni). This work incorporates video image processing using the Sandin analog IP and Datamax UV1 graphics system (ZGrass programming language).

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nnNK1IUdD6c


Eat Meat
(1984)
     This is an example of early computer animation created by Dana Plepys using the Datamax UV1 system, ZGrass programming language developed at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory at the University of Illinois at Chicago. The video incorporates unique morphing, which was new to computer graphics at the time.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vw2ebTkROBs


Floater Final Sequence
(1983)
     This is an example of early computer graphics animation developed by Jane Veeder at the Electronic Visualization Lab, using the Datamax UV1 graphics system and ZGrass programming language.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2GQJtmgaNIg


Only Eyes
(1983)
     This is an example of early computer graphics animation developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab using the Datamax UV-1. This animation was developed by Maggie Rawlings.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SXwLcNxnshA


Paint Piece
(1983)
     This is an example of early computer graphics animation developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab using the Datamax UV-1. This animation was developed by Mark McKernin. [This looks "too hi-res" to really be on the UV-1 to me.  Adam]

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WlvADQNFaQQ


P.I. Piece
(1983)
     This is an example of early computer graphics animation developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab using the Datamax UV-1. This animation was developed by Mark McKernin.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hxqqhqizJjU


Ralph the Punk
(1985)
     This is an example of early video animation developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab using the Datamax UV-1. This video was developed by Charlie Athanas and Johnie Hugh Horn.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZSuooSGgILo


Real Time Design, Inc. Zgrass Demo (1:05)
(1982)
     This is one of the movies that document the early history of the research that resulted in the creation of the EVL Lab.
     This is a demo with several shorts, showing the image manipulation capabilities of the the GRASS3 language that was designed to run on the Z Box. The language then became known a Zgrass. This video and the content were created by Thomas DeFanti, Daniel Sandin, Copper Giloth, Jane Veeder at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wosAsPyspsU


Return to Planet Claire (1981)
     This is an example of early computer graphics animation developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab using the Datamax UV-1 and Zgrass. This video was created by Sue Forner and Rick Frankel.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sdcKDhzC9u4


Skippy Peanut Butter Jars
(1980)
     This is a demo of early computer graphics animation using the Datamax UV-1 and the Zgrass programing language, developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab. This video demo was created by Copper Giloth.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cllp-71fJos


Two Boxes at Once
(1979) Bally Arcade
     This is an example of early computer graphics animation on the Datamax UV-1, developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab. This animation was created by Mark McKernin.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YAneQGhILBg


Warpitout
(1982)
     This is an example of early computer graphics animation developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab. This video was created by Jane Veeder.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcU1LyGdg3k


Zgrass Paint Demo (1:30)
(1980)
     This is one of the movies that document the early history of the research that resulted in the creation of the EVL Lab.
     Tom Defanti presents a demo of the Zgrass paint application for use on the Datamax UV-1.
     The basis for the Datamax UV-1 was the GRASS programing language, originally developed by Tom DeFanti for his 1974 Ohio State University Ph.D. thesis.
     The GRASS language was further developed into the GRASS3 language that was designed to run on the Z Box. The language then became known a Zgrass.
     The Z-Box was a raster graphics machine, unlike the original GRASS systems, so while most of the GRASS3 style was maintained in Zgrass, it added a number of commands dedicated to raster images.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xiPPVvtX91o

What I'm looking at is how many people could purchase the item (expanded RAM owners) and perhaps a few people that buy the item for it to go up in value.  I'm saying that throwing in a few extras like professional printed manuals, labels and boxes would go a LONG way toward justifying a $250 purchase in the buyer's mind.

>>
I am planning on selling about 20 units
>>

How many Lil' Blue RAM units have sold?  Other than that amount, there are only about five people with working RAM units for the Astrocade.  That's your market.

>>
$25.00 ea. for a new 8 Meg chip
$20.00 ea. for newly designed printed circuit board

>>

$71 in parts and materials.

>>
Now let's evaluate how much each cartridge would cost if you bought it at today's prices.
>>

The person who buys the multicart is NOT getting the original cartridges that you refer to. They are getting COPIES.  Ward Shrake, when discussing his multicart in 2001, comes right out and says that he couldn't charge for the games on his multicart because he does not own the rights to them.

>>
Next, let's look at the many programs that have NEVER been a part of the public domain.
>>

>>
Then there is the engineering time, assembling and programming.
>>

I'm not underestimating the time that it took to create this project.  I'm POSITIVE that it took a LONG time.

>>
Do you all think I should be going negative?
>>

Of course not.  I would like you to make a profit.  I LOVE that you are making these items for the Astrocade community.  I'm just a bit afraid that you might be overestimating how large the Astrocade community is, and how much it might be willing to pay for a multicart.  If you sell twenty of your multicarts cartridges for $250 I will be VERY happy for you; I will be glad to see that the Astrocade community is so healthy.

Adam

I asked Ward Shrake about this thoughts on the multicart subject.  He can't post directly right now, so I'm posting his thoughts for him.  He has NOT read the posts about the multicart; he only know that there is a new multicart.  Here are his comments about it:


Hour-per-hour, $250 is probably cheap -- if this other person is doing it at all like I did mine, anyway. But still ... no one seems to want to pay for hours and hours of skilled labor, at the Skilled Labor going-rates. Buyers want to pay the cheapest possible price a mass-produced widget would cost ... even if it's the farthest thing away from being a mass produced item. I see it as a disconnect from reality, on both the buyer's and seller's parts. I don't see either the sellers "winning," or the buyers "winning" ... which is one big reason that I'm no longer interested in making things that take skilled labor and many hours, to sell to the public. I'm not the only one. In one of my other hobbies, I see skilled people talking about their projects all the time. People always say, "Ooh, ooh; I want it! How much!?" ... and then freak out, or slink away, when the builder quotes them a price that won't end in their homelessness. One guy in particular (the owner of the SubPirates dot com scale modeling forum) simply says pretty much what I've been saying for years: not gonna do it, except for fun or friends.

5855:
The prices for the cartridges on eBay are ridiculous.  Note that none (or at most few) of these are sold.  If the cartridges or machines could be sold for those prices, I would have dumped all of mine long ago.  I would disregard them.
   
  For a quality manual of instructions for all known programs and cartridges alone, I think this would be worth a good amount and could be sold separately from the multicart even to people who do not buy the multicart.  In fact, even a multicart buyer might want two or more.  Those should be created and built and priced separately.  I would think $25 would be reasonable for a quality manual with multiple copies bought at the same time or with a multicart cheaper.
   
  As far as for the cartidge itself, I have always (or at least for the last few decades) trusted Ken's judgement to not build or sell junk.  He claims about $60 in cost for parts.  I would imagine at least another $60 for his time assembling and a pro-rata cost of engineering and design.  Then, I would want Ken to have sufficient profit to make him (or anyone) want to produce something else for my Astrocade.  Let's assume doubling the cost for a small run in order to make it profitable enough.  That comes to $240 plus a manual for $25 plus perhaps $10 for shipping and handling.  This comes to $275, so from my perspective, I can't quibble with the original price mentioned.
   
  From a buyer's perspective, it is very different.  If I want every Astrocade product, price doesn't matter.  If I want to use it for games and I have few or none and the real games are harder to find or more costly, I still like the price.  However, if you are one of the real old-timers who had bought all of the cartridges you could get your hands on or afford back when they were at JS&A, and Wards and Wall Street Camera, this is like another archive to go with your Ward Shrake and Retrokids cartridges for just in case the real cartridge dies.  For those buyers, the price is steep and the value lies in the additional software that is unavailable elsewhere in cartridge form.  Whether that software is worth the additional cost, I don't really know.
   
  However, for the show price, you are talking about a $300 new in the box Astrocade (one just sold for that price on eBay [unlike the cartridges which never sell]) plus two extra controllers ($29.95 was the list price on these back in the old days) which I have seen offered for around $30, you are suggesting paying people $30 to take the multicart.  Assuming the cost to assemble and build remains $120, this means a loss of $150 on that one cartridge.  It seems to make me wonder if I have overpriced it in the above analysis.

The prices for the cartridges on eBay are ridiculous.  Note that none (or at
most few) of these are sold.  If the cartridges or machines could be sold
for those prices, I would have dumped all of mine long ago.  I would
disregard them.
 
For a quality manual of instructions for all known programs and cartridges
alone, I think this would be worth a good amount and could be sold
separately from the multicart even to people who do not buy the multicart.
In fact, even a multicart buyer might want two or more.  Those should be
created and built and priced separately.  I would think $25 would be
reasonable for a quality manual with multiple copies bought at the same time
or with a multicart cheaper.
 
As far as for the cartidge itself, I have always (or at least for the last
few decades) trusted Ken's judgement to not build or sell junk.  He claims
about $60 in cost for parts.  I would imagine at least another $60 for his
time assembling and a pro-rata cost of engineering and design.  Then, I
would want Ken to have sufficient profit to make him (or anyone) want to
produce something else for my Astrocade.  Let's assume doubling the cost for
a small run in order to make it profitable enough.  That comes to $240 plus
a manual for $25 plus perhaps $10 for shipping and handling.  This comes to
$275, so from my perspective, I can't quibble with the original price
mentioned.
 
From a buyer's perspective, it is very different.  If I want every Astrocade
product, price doesn't matter.  If I want to use it for games and I have few
or none and the real games are harder to find or more costly, I still like
the price.  However, if you are one of the real old-timers who had bought
all of the cartridges you could get your hands on or afford back when they
were at JS&A, and Wards and Wall Street Camera, this is like another archive
to go with your Ward Shrake and Retrokids cartridges for just in case the
real cartridge dies.  For those buyers, the price is steep and the value
lies in the additional software that is unavailable elsewhere in cartridge
form.  Whether that software is worth the additional cost, I don't really
know.
 
However, for the show price, you are talking about a $300 new in the box
Astrocade (one just sold for that price on eBay [unlike the cartridges which
never sell]) plus two extra controllers ($29.95 was the list price on these
back in the old days) which I have seen offered for around $30, you are
suggesting paying people $30 to take the multicart.  Assuming the cost to
assemble and build remains $120, this means a loss of $150 on that one
cartridge.  It seems to make me wonder if I have overpriced it in the above
analysis.

Bill Loguidice wrote:
>>

I partially agree with you, though the rest of the reviews in the book don't differ
that much from these few review that I've added so far.  The author crams a LOT
of games into the book.  Some of the game review are MUCH longer, and I think
that's because he enjoyed the games and decided to write strategy guides (in the
loosest sense of the meaning) about the games.  I give that he may never even have
SEEN "Quest for the Orbs," but it does seem as though he played Muncher (reviewed
as "Munchie") and played around with "Music Maker."

The book has reviews for most Bally games, with Galactic Invasion being, by FAR,
the longest (he really liked that game!).  He skims over some cartridges that I would
have expected a deeper review of.  For instance, Bally BASIC is compared with
the Atari 2600 "BASIC Programming" and Odyssey 2's "Computer Intro."  There
isn't even mention that Bally BASIC could save programs when compared to the
other cartridges.  I think that the reviewer played the cartridges that he liked best
and used the book as an excuse, perhaps, to get free cartridges and make some
money on the side.  I'm not knocking him.  Heck, that's a SMART idea.

On a side note, Jeff Rovin's "The Complete Guide to Conquering Video Games: How
to Win Every Game in the Galaxy" is not a one-hit wonder.  He wrote literally dozens
of game books, many of them for the Nintendo.  It seems that he had a formula, and
he used it to his advantage!

Does anyone have much experience with his other books?

--- In ballyalley@yahoogroups.com, "Mike White" <mike@...> wrote:
>
> Tell me though, what would you consider
> a fair price if you were selling a new item?

Once again, I'm just throwing my two cents in here, for consideration.
I'm not commenting back to specific people -- just watching for key
phrases, and using them as an excuse to talk more about that idea.

I am not saying "do something specific" or "don't do that thing". I'm
just adding some comments, based on my experiences with making items
that very few people either knew how to make; or were willing to make.

First off, strike "fair price" from your thinking, in this situation.
Collectors (speculators, really) are NOT interested in giving ANYONE "a
fair price". They're interested in making a killing; which means they
win and you lose. Notice all the talk about price ... versus next to no
talk at all, about "tell me more about these games I'd get to play".

Besides any other considerations, I think that the "let's charge over
$200" thinking may have been influenced by what my multicarts go for,
at present: which, I'm told, is around the $200 range. Keep in mind
that the only time I received over $100 for one of my multicarts was
one of the very last ones ever made; auctioned off; and advertised (if
my aging memory serves) as being the last one that I'd ever sell. It
also included (partially to puncuate that "no more" point) assembly
jigs that I once used, to make the ones I'd made, previous to that.

My point is this: collectors, in my opinion, LOVE the idea of
a "starving artist". What they love even more is getting several of the
artistic objects being made ... at a price that INSURES you starve!
Why? Because they have much more greed than empathy. If you literally
drop dead, after they've bought up your inventory ... it's Profit City!
But as long as you're "alive" and functioning as an artist, what they
have isn't anywhere near as saleable. Or at least, not at above what
some might call "a fair price".

Balancing that out is some folks that (arguably) have more money than
sense; and will buy all sorts of things that they'll never recoup their
money on, if they ever try to re-sell those objects. And some of them
have no intent of ever re-selling what they buy. But they're rare types
of people. (There is also a third group that WILL pay a "fair price,"
and do so without making the seller's life miserable. Bless them all!)

Nevertheless, my point about the $200+ asking price for a Ward Shrake
multicart is that I didn't make that much. That's double what I got for
them, in all but one case (mentioned above). I grossed $100 at first;
and later $85 gross per cart. Subtract parts cost, etc., and we're at a
price point where I'd literally be better off, flipping burgers. So for
that and many other reasons, I quit making them. Bam! Double the
price ... but someone else is making that double-their-money profit.

5896:
The only thing I disagree with is the constant reference to Burger
King-style wages.  I appreciate the amount of effort that goes into these
things, but the reason can't be to make any type of reasonable hourly wage,
it has to be for the challenge, for the notoriety, for the "legendary
status", etc., essentially all intangibles.  I think I mentioned it here
before.  I can make it analogous in some way to freelance writing,
particularly book writing.  For all the effort that goes into it, I could
never make even a fraction of what my hourly wage is actually worth - in
fact what I can make for the actual work might be change per hour, frankly,
at best, but I don't do it for the money.  My "real" job is for the money,
and for that I insist on a real wage for obvious reasons.  For something I'm
doing for the passion of it, for something I love, I'm far more forgiving
with putting far more effort than I'll ever hope to make back in any
tangible sense.  To me, that's what this and all other non-mass market
productions have to be about - making enough where you don't actually lose
money, but certainly not something where you're to justify some type of
monetary equation-it's just not going to work out.  

 

Again, I fall firmly in the category of supporting homebrew stuff through
purchases that I'll never sell - I collect for myself.  I have limits though
and if something is out of range, I simply can't do it, no matter how much I
want the product.  I want this product, but it's out of my range for
something like this and for that I'm sad.  But you know what, I don't NEED
it, do I?  All I can offer is my opinion that I think it's priced too high
and the market is too small and leave it at that.  I have no horse in the
race as it were.  I want to see it succeed and I want one for myself, but
most likely I won't be getting one for myself.  Fair enough.

5898:
Bill, Mike: I really like your recent comments. Now we're approaching
what I see as a realistic appraisal of the situation.

To me, any talk of "How much profit can I make, on this hobby?" is,
at best, a justification for the unspoken internal realization that
maybe, just maybe, the hobby quit being fun ... as it stood, before.

Realistically, as soon as you say "I spent a year working on this;
but I won't count that in the loss column; so I'll just ignore that,
and focus on other factors, and try to trick my book-keeper into
believing that I can still make a financial gain from doing this" ...
you may as well sell all you have, and take up smoking crack. (Or 
ingesting whatever the latest designer drug is; I try not to know.)


Others will discount everything I've said as meaningless drivel, or
sour grapes. So be it. But to me, here's the Very Bottom Bottomline:

The central myth of consumer culture is that the more items you own,
and the cooler those items are, the more other people will like you;
love you; look up to you; want to be you; will worship you as a God.

The truth, as I see it, is just the opposite: the more you have, and
the cooler each item is, the more people will hate you.

They want it. You have it. They don't. Therefore, you're the bad guy;
they're the good guy; and if they are not happy, the vast majority of
rabid consumers in any consumer culture, will blame that unhappiness
on you. Which, personally, I think is insane. But that's just me.

My last words on this subject will be ....

I didn't "drop" the Bally Astrocade, or even retro-gaming: I dropped
the idea that owning stuff could make an unhappy person happy, on a
long-term basis. Acquiring something new is only a temporary high;
you will need another fix, and another, and another, in short order.

Sad to say, yes. But the way I see it, that's the way things are. And
the only ones that benefit are the middlemen, who buy cheap and sell
dear. The makers of the items won't profit. Neither will the buyers.



It took me forty years to figure out my Top Ten Priorities. Here they
are, in ranked order.

Life.
Health.
Water.
Food.
Clothing.
Shelter.
Medicines; as needed.
Medical care; as needed.

Those eight things I have to have, before I can pursue the next two:

Leisure Time.
Serenity.


Just food for thought, guys. It's offered freely; and worth far more.


There's some benefit to be had from a hobby ... but to me, if it is
not closely aligned to those two last things, it could be dangerous.
My advice is to know exactly WHY you're doing what you're doing; and
don't deceive yourself as to either the costs of it; or the benefits.

You only have one life. Spend every hour as wisely as you can.

 -- Ward Shrake --

2008_02_24 - Life Article - Two articles from about "Life" from Scientific American.

2008_02_29 - Frames - This is work that I would like to use to re-do the screenshots area.  Currently, I really dislike the way that the area is set-up and I want it to be more functional.

2008_03_06 - RetroKidz Multicart Dipswitch Listing - A Dipswitch listing of Richard's Degler's RetroKidz Astrocade multicart.

2008_03_08 - Memory test - BASIC listings of Memory testers in BASIC.

2008_03_13 - Decomposer - A program listing for Richard Degler's program.

2008_04_20 - Replacement Character Font for use with Blue Ram Basic 1.1 - I need to test this before I upload it.

2008_04_28 - Cursor and FAQ Updates - Suggestions (that I'm going to take) by Paul Thacker of updates that I need to make to FAQ and the Cursor section.

2008_05_03 - Astrocade Poster - A poster of the Astrocade that I can't work-with myself.  The poster needs to be stitched together from several different files.  If you have experience in this area, then it would be great if you could volunteer for this project.
2008_05_03 - Marketing Materials - Fourteen documents that Paul Thacker scanned in that I need to figure-out where to add to the website.

2008_05_05 - Color BASIC WAV - A "tape" version of ColorBASIC that should load into an expanded RAM system.  I need to test this before I upload it.

Astrocade_Instructions_Needed.txt - A list of instructions that Paul Thacker made back in January that needs to be added instruction area of the website.

Color BASIC - 2008 02 09.txt - Reminder to myself to make a recording of a short program in Color BASIC with :PRINT; LIST for Paul Thacker.

Create Pictures and Review of Lil' Blue Ram.txt - Reminder to myself to review and take pictures of the Lil' White RAM.

Once the above is completed, then I'll be caught up with the backlog of material to add to Ballyalley.com.  After that, there is literally YEARS worth of scanning material that I got from the Robert Fabris lot.  I also need to take pictures of some of the hardware that I have for the Astrocade (Computer Ear, BalCheck, keyboard and other miscellaneous items).  Then there is another directory that I have called "to_finish" with ideas and unfinished articles that I don't even like to LOOK in!

I was thinking that "one of these days" I'll be caught up, but then I thought, part of the fun aspect of this is that there is still so much to do after all of these years.  The Bally/Atrocade is truly are remarkable system!

5940:
I would like to add a "Memory Lane" section to Ballyalley.com.  This would consist of stories sent in by Bally Arcade/Astrocade users.  Do you have some memories that you would like to share?  To help get your noggin working, think about ideas like this:

1) Did you stay up all night in 1980 playing a game that you just couldn't keep your hands off of and even today you're afraid to admit that it was "Bingo Math?"

2) Did you program fifty different versions of a BASIC program that just used the INPUT command to ask a person's name or age?

3) Did you get together with friends in your neighborhood to test each other's reflexes with games that, like "The Incredible Wizard," just BLEW AWAY conversions of games for your friend's game systems?

4) Were you a subscriber to the Arcadian who just couldn't get enough of that good stuff?

5) Did you wait for YEARS for the add-under to come out and then finally bought another computer instead?

6) Did you wear out your joysticks-- or even worse, did you wear out your Astrocade?

7) Did you have an Astrocade and an Atari 2600 and an Intellivision, and to you, they they were all equal; they all had great games that you liked to play?

8) Did you tell your friends about this "great system" that you had but no one had ever heard of it?

9) Did you consider the Bally Arcade a computer and not a game console at all?

10) Did you play games with the whole family while other families were playing Monopoly and Risk?

11) Did the Astrocade end up having some profound influence on your life?

12) Did you use the Astrocade in some unusual manner that you just couldn't have done with any other system at the same price?

13) Did you buy a 4K Blue Ram unit and think that you'd now NEVER run out of memory?

14) Did you only hear of the Astrocade when you saw one just a few years ago at a garage sale / flea market / thrift store and you picked it up just because you collect all the classic systems?

If you would like to share any memories of yourself, please post 'em here and they will make their way to Ballyalley.com.

I look forward to hearing some FUN, NEAT and maybe even just some downright WEIRD experiences!

Adam

5951:
I spoke to Mike White on the phone last night and he told me about a misconception that at least one person has with the Lil' White Ram and Astrocade multicarts.  I just want to clear it up here in case anyone else has this confusion too.

1) All of the multicarts seem to have a different amount of programs that require expanded RAM (some may have none-- I've not used all of the multicarts).  Only Ken's most recent release seems to have EVERYTHING.

2) It is NOT possible to buy a Lil' White Ram, or use a RAM expansion of any sort, to play the expanded RAM games available for download on Ballyalley.com.  This isn't because these devices can't use programs loaded from tape, but because the games are NOT archived (on Ballyalley.com or anyplace else).  There is currently only ONE expanded RAM program that is archived, and that is the "Viper Test Pattern."  Now that the Lil' White Ram is available these programs can begin to be archived.  Expanded RAM programs were not digitally archived earlier because there was no way to test the archived programs on really equipment (since it is so rare).

In summary, if you want to play all of the expanded RAM games, then you have only one option: buy the Lil' White Ram and Ken's new multicart.  Then you can play EVERYTHING.

Adam

Group;

It goes further than that! I just got back from CCAGshow and have
quite a bit to tell now that the show's over for now.

The biggest news from the show is that the next show is scheduled for
12 OCT 08 (THIS YEAR!) not MAY 09! This will be the first time that
any CCAGshow happened twice in the same year! Although not on thier
website yet, if anyone can make it, mark your calender. It will be at
the same place and time "SAME BAT TIME, SAME BAT CHANNEL" as they say!

To really understand shows, one would really have to go to them, and
exhibiters see even more than that. First off, everything posted on
this group WAS known by venders and buyers alike at CCAGshow! In
other words, to post something on this discussion group is the same
as having it broadcast on CNN as far as the show community is
concerned!

For instance, not since 2004 (I believe) was there another Bally
Arcade at a show, UNTILL NOW! Message 5816 says that Arcades could
have been sold at the show Toby attended recently. GUESS WHAT! My
luck is such that as soon as I get ready to sell something, so is
everybody else!

Another rule about shows is the "cruse" principle. It works like
this. When a buyer enters the show, he begins by "crusing". That is
by going from booth to booth to booth to booth to booth etc. until
he's visited, spoke with, and gotten prices from EVERY vender in the
place! Then he returns to the one with the lowest price and buys
there, or asks the vender to "demo" the item to see if it's DOA! If
it is he moves on to the next lowest priced vender and repeats. This
means that the guy who is unloading, say, a liquidation inventory
(estate sale where some collector died, or a shop that bellyed up)
and doesn't know or care what his items are worth, has the advantage
of being the lowest priced vender! Consequently, one hour into the
show he leaves behind an empty table with his pockets bulging! The
vender that appears as the most expensive to the "crusers" drags
EVERYTHING home that he brought and can't even cover the rental fee
on his table! Is this in any way "fair pricing"? OF COURSE NOT!!! But
that's what happens at shows! This is why you really can't compare
show prices to those found elsewhere. To even have a chance of
recovering your table fee you have to lower your price to what others
outside of show circles would find hard to understand. (As it was, I
took Adams advice, separated everything, and still finished LAST!)
Which brings me to another aspect of showing, the "bundle".

Sometimes a vender will sell everything he's got by dumping
everything in a loose box and telling buyers $1.00 per item!
Sometimes he will sell a "package" that consists of something like I
origionally proposed doing (the $300.00 offer) that Adam talked me
out of. I'm still not sure (from a sellers perspective) which is
better, because if there is something in the "bundle" that the buyer
really wants, now he has to pay more for it because he has to buy the
entire "bundle" instead of one $1.00 item. Collectors don't care (it
seems) how big the "bundle" is, or how much it costs, they may still
buy it, take it out to the parking lot, open it up, take out the
desired item, toss the rest in the dumpster, and drive home with
thier prize!!! Does this make any sense at all? OF COURSE NOT!! But
that's what happenes at shows! This is why you can't even compare one
show to another, one buyer to another, it even changes one hour to
another!! That's why it's ALL IMPORTANT to have some idea exactly
what your stuff is worth TODAY!! NOT YESTERDAY OR LAST WEEK!!! This
changes rapidly (especially where a show is involved) which is
usually WAY DIFFERENT from what you believed it to be when you walked
in. Frustrating? Absolutely!

So then, why go? TO HAVE FUN!!! When I go I set up TWO machines
(demonstrators I call them), put chairs out front, and let attendees
play! One is a very old PC that evolved from a 386 16mhz to a 486
60mhz and on to a Pentium 133mhz. But in all those changes, it never
had the CMOS ROM upgraded and STILL thinks it's 1998! It never saw
Windows, not even version 0.0000001 (even if there was such an early
prototype) and runs as a DOS computer. To upgrade to something that
COULD EVEN be seriously considered "usable" would cost more than
buying a new unit! Therefore, what good is it? It plays ID's DOOM
like hot peppers! And at a game show, that's all that counts! Between
that and a Bally Arcade (also running constantly) I usually have
someone in front of my booth going at something! Some kid will see
the units running and say to a parent "DADDY CAN I PLAY?" whereas the
parent will repeat the question to me and I will respond "SURE, TEAR
IT UP KID!". What happens in the next 2 seconds is what I go to these
shows for!

There's much more to be said about this past CCAGshow, especially the
influnce that this message board has on it. But now that it's over
there can be some questions answered, beginning by what Adam started
to say. I was asked at the show if the CARTRIDGE GAMES on Bally Alley
could be used in a real Arcade. I then tried to explain how a LIL'
WHITE RAM could do it, but was interrupted and asked if the entire
library could be loaded at once. I said "no, only one at a time", the
prospective buyer then said "forget it! I'll just have to get a
$59.95 multicart instead". (Where did he hear about the $59.95
multicart? As I said, this message board is being closely watched!)

A rumor circulating at present is that the RETROKIDS multicart
is "upgradeable for FREE"! I think this got started by someone
putting message numbers 5902, 5929, and 5930 together. I never
understood it to be that interpretation. How about a comment here?

As that is, it'll be impossible to sell BALLY WAR if buyers (show
mentality) would rather wait until it appears on a multicart in a
FREE upgrade than pay say, $20.00 for a single cartridge, no matter
how good it's touted!

Another rumor is the one that says "there is ABSOLUTELY NO Bally
Arcades ON PLANET EARTH anymore that work"! Even having mine run for
over 4 hours and kids playing the games didn't convince some. They
kept asking if I repaired Arcades and this was a special one that
I "RIGGED" to run for the show, or this was by chance a "NEW" Arcade
from somewhere (perhaps a high res unit as per Jim Kritch). This is
SO NOT TRUE! BELIEVE IT OR NOT!! As to Jim, he was out of state, and
didn't make it to this show at all. I look to see him at the next 
show (on Columbus Day 2008).

Yes I could really go on talking about this year's CCAGshow, but I'll
save the rest for another time. Except to say that I now have THREE
prospective buyers for my ASTRO BLASTER. (I own an upright coin op
version of the Gremlin game, but perhaps not for long).

Mike W.
